Muse runs in a Secure VM—a virtual machine, or a dedicated cloud computer where Muse works and stores its data. Muse proposes an action; a separate control layer called Sentinel checks its permission and network request before it reaches a connected service.

A fresh approval does not appear before everything. Meta says a person can let Muse read email without letting it send. Permissions may be one-time, limited to a task or session, time-bounded or permanent; Sentinel chooses which options to offer. Previously allowed, read-only or low-risk actions may proceed without interruption. Email and purchase prompts are Meta’s design, not a guarantee that Muse always behaves correctly.

Meta’s safety post says the agent will make mistakes and that prompt injection—malicious instructions hidden in material an agent reads—remains an open problem. AP confirmed the launch and explained the agent-versus-chatbot distinction, but did not test Muse’s safeguards or reliability.

Today’s Secure VM isolates each person’s agent and data and hides credentials from the agent. Meta says it may still access data to operate, support or secure the service. It also says interaction records may train later models after personal details are removed unless the person opts out. Confidential VM, intended to block even Meta’s access cryptographically, remains with trusted testers and is planned for later this year.

Meta launched Muse, a personal AI agent, in the United States on September 8. It is rolling out through iOS, Android and muse.ai; Meta also says people can message it in WhatsApp. Most use is free, with subscriptions for more, but the reviewed launch material gives no exact limit or price.

Unlike a chatbot that stops after suggesting or drafting, Muse is designed to keep taking steps through a browser and connected services. Meta says it can continue after the app closes. AI glasses support, Shop Pay, 1Password support and a stronger privacy mode are later plans.

A personal AI agent is software that can plan and take several actions toward a personal goal rather than only answer once. In Meta’s example, Muse could turn an Instagram recipe into a grocery list without email access; sending the dinner invitation requires connected email and permission to send.

sources.authority: Meta primary release for Muse's September 8 launch, current United States availability, access routes, product actions, pricing boundary and announced roadmap.
passages: September 8, 2026
Muse is a personal AI agent. It doesn’t just answer questions, it actually does the work.
Muse is designed around the way people already communicate, so talking to it works just like messaging another person, in the Muse app or directly in WhatsApp.
It can open a browser, fill out forms, and negotiate on their behalf.
For tasks that take more time, Muse keeps working after people close the app, and comes back when something changes or when it needs approval, like before it sends an email or makes a purchase.
People choose which apps Muse connects to and exactly how much access it gets.
For things like email, people choose what Muse can do, whether it reads their mail or can also send on their behalf.
Muse shows people a complete audit trail of everything it has done and plans to do.
People can also opt out of their interactions being used to train Meta’s AI models.

Later this year, Meta will introduce Muse Confidential VM, where the whole VM, including a person’s data and conversations with Muse, is encrypted with a key only they hold, so not even Meta can access it.
Muse is rolling out in the US on iOS, Android, and muse.ai , and coming soon to AI glasses.
It’s free for most of what people need, with subscription plans for people who want to do more.
Shop Pay is coming soon as another way to pay, along with 1Password support so Muse can use logins a person already has.
sources.limitation: This is Meta's product announcement. It establishes what Meta launched and promised, but does not independently establish reliability, security outcomes, adoption or a universal ability to complete every named task.

source.passage: September 8, 2026 Muse is a personal AI agent. It doesn’t just answer questions, it actually does the work. Muse is designed around the way people already communicate, so talking to it works just like messaging another person, in the Muse app or directly in WhatsApp. It can open a browser, fill out forms, and negotiate on their behalf. For tasks that take more time, Muse keeps working after people close the app, and comes back when something changes or when it needs approval, like before it sends an email or makes a purchase. People choose which apps Muse connects to and exactly how much access it gets. For things like email, people choose what Muse can do, whether it reads their mail or can also send on their behalf. Muse shows people a complete audit trail of everything it has done and plans to do. People can also opt out of their interactions being used to train Meta’s AI models. Later this year, Meta will introduce Muse Confidential VM, where the whole VM, including a person’s data and conversations with Muse, is encrypted with a key only they hold, so not even Meta can access it. Muse is rolling out in the US on iOS, Android, and muse.ai , and coming soon to AI glasses. It’s free for most of what people need, with subscription plans for people who want to do more. Shop Pay is coming soon as another way to pay, along with 1Password support so Muse can use logins a person already has.

sources.authority: Meta primary technical account of the launch architecture, permissions, current data practices, acknowledged fallibility and planned Confidential VM.
passages: It was also the first time we’d handed our inboxes, our calendars, and a shell to a piece of software and let it run unattended — which didn’t always work out as planned.
No matter how strong the model is at the core, any agent like this will still make mistakes, and it will sometimes be attacked via the data it reads.
Muse can and will still make mistakes, but we expect they’ll be much less frequent and cause much less damage due to the safety systems we’ve built in.
Muse clients (the iOS and Android apps, the web UI) connect directly to your VM via a secure transport layer.
Sentinel is the sole permission authority for connector actions and network egress.
Muse proposes actions, but only Sentinel can grant permission to perform action.
Muse has support for obtaining one-time, session-scoped, task-scoped, time-bounded, or perpetual permission.
Sentinel decides which grant types to present for the user to choose between and ensures that subsequent invocations match the granted scope exactly.
Read-only, previously allowed, or demonstrably low-risk actions can proceed without interruption.
It restricts access to your data by Meta personnel through operational policies. It does not prevent Meta from accessing data when necessary to support, secure or operate the service.
If you do not want your data to be used in model training at all, you can opt-out via a simple switch in Muse settings.
Muse Confidential VM is intended to cryptographically and verifiably prevent Meta from accessing data in your VM.
We’re already using this system with a small group of trusted testers
Muse isn’t immune to attack. Prompt injection remains an open problem in the industry — and Muse will sometimes make mistakes.
sources.limitation: This is Meta's own engineering explanation, not an independent audit or proof that the controls always work. The Confidential VM is described as a future capability under testing.
